title: Totally tubeless simultaneous bilateral VATS for pulmonary fungal granulomas following solid organ transplantation.
authors: Fan C, Liang Z, Sang G et al.
abstract:
BACKGROUND: Radiologically differentiating opportunistic pulmonary fungal infections from lung malignancies after solid organ transplantation (SOT) is difficult. Although a surgical biopsy is often required for definitive diagnosis, conventional intubated general anesthesia and routine chest tube drainage increase the risk of nosocomial infections and complications in immunosuppressed patients. Simultaneous bilateral completely tubeless video-assisted thoracoscopic surgery (VATS)-performed without endotracheal intubation or postoperative chest drains-is an advanced Enhanced Recovery After Surgery (ERAS) approach that could mitigate these risks. However, clinical experience with this technique in SOT recipients remains scarce.
CASE PRESENTATION: A 64-year-old male liver transplant recipient on long-term sirolimus presented with incidental pulmonary nodules. He had a limited 5-year smoking history (10 cigarettes/day), and his routine antiplatelet therapy (aspirin) was held preoperatively. Chest CT revealed a solid right upper lobe nodule and a cavitary left upper lobe nodule. Both lesions displayed spiculated margins and pleural indentation, raising high suspicion for malignancy (synchronous primary lung cancers and/or pulmonary metastases). The patient underwent simultaneous bilateral tubeless VATS wedge resections. Surgery was performed under regional anesthesia with spontaneous ventilation via a laryngeal mask airway (LMA). Estimated blood loss was 20 mL. After bilateral resection and negative water-seal tests, the temporary chest tubes were removed directly on the operating table. Final pathology confirmed chronic fungal granulomatous inflammation. A postoperative day (POD) 1 chest radiograph showed near-complete bilateral lung expansion with a minimal left pneumothorax and mild localized atelectasis. The patient remained asymptomatic, requiring no pleural interventions. Managed under standard ERAS protocols, he recovered uneventfully and was discharged on POD 4.
CONCLUSION: Chronic immunosuppression can induce local fibrosis that causes pulmonary fungal infections to radiologically mimic malignancies. For high-risk solid organ transplantation (SOT) recipients, simultaneous bilateral tubeless VATS may represent a potential diagnostic and therapeutic strategy. Avoiding chest tubes minimizes potential pathways for nosocomial infection. Concurrently, preserving spontaneous ventilation may facilitate physiological recovery, allowing for the safe, conservative observation of minor postoperative radiological abnormalities.

title: The immune landscape of chordoma and opportunities for immunotherapy.
authors: Jonathan SV, Gellert J, Wu X et al.
abstract:
PURPOSE: Chordoma is a rare, locally aggressive tumor arising from notochordal remnants with limited effective systemic treatment options. Growing interest in immunotherapy has prompted investigation of the chordoma tumor immune microenvironment (TIME) and the development of immunotherapeutic strategies targeting its molecular and cellular components. This review synthesizes the current literature on the immune landscape of chordoma and evaluates the clinical evidence and translational rationale for immunotherapeutic strategies in this disease.
METHODS: A PRISMA-compliant systematic search of the ClinicalTrials.gov registry was conducted using disease- and immunotherapy-specific search terms. Records were screened for trials explicitly enrolling chordoma patients and investigating immunotherapy, including immune checkpoint inhibitors (ICIs), tumor-associated antigen vaccines, oncolytic platforms, and adoptive cellular therapies. Supplementary literature review identified additional trials not captured in the registry search.
RESULTS: Thirty clinical trials evaluating immunotherapy in chordoma were identified. The chordoma TIME is spatially compartmentalized, with tumor-associated macrophages (TAMs) as the dominant infiltrating immune population and effector T cells physically excluded from the tumor parenchyma. A clinically relevant subset of tumors harbor inflamed transcriptional states and clonally enriched T cell receptor repertoires, consistent with antigen-driven immune activity that is suppressed rather than absent. ICI-based strategies, particularly PD-1 blockade, have demonstrated durable disease control in a meaningful subset of patients. Brachyury-directed vaccines have established immunogenicity but have not consistently translated to objective responses. Oncolytic virotherapy has produced isolated responses in early-phase trials, whereas NK cell-engaging antibody strategies and B7-H3-directed CAR-T cells remain preclinical.
CONCLUSION: Chordoma is not immunologically inert, but its immune-excluded TIME, macrophage-dominant immunosuppressive milieu, and low tumor mutational burden present distinct barriers to conventional immunotherapy. Given chordoma's indolent biology, objective response rate may underestimate clinical benefit, whereas disease control rate and progression-free survival are most interpretable in randomized trials or in single-arm trials requiring documented progression at enrollment. Biomarker-driven patient selection integrating tumor genomics, spatial immune architecture, and checkpoint expression will be essential for advancing rational combination immunotherapy in this disease.

title: Precision Immunotherapy for Pediatric Medulloblastoma: Integrating Tumor Immune Microenvironment, Molecular Heterogeneity, and Cellular Therapy.
authors: Zhang X, Du L, Tian K et al.
abstract: Medulloblastoma (MB) is the most common malignant pediatric brain tumor and remains a major cause of cancer-related morbidity and mortality in children. Although multimodal therapies have significantly improved survival for many patients, children with high-risk, metastatic, or recurrent MB continue to face limited therapeutic options and severe treatment-related complications. Immunotherapy has emerged as a promising strategy. However, clinical responses to conventional immune-based approaches, particularly immune checkpoint blockade, have been modest due to the low immunogenicity, immunosuppressive tumor immune microenvironment (TIME), and substantial molecular heterogeneity of MB. Recent advances in single-cell sequencing, spatial profiling, and molecular classification have revealed that MB consists of distinct biological entities with unique immune landscapes and therapeutic vulnerabilities. These findings have shifted the field from nonspecific immune activation toward precision-guided immunotherapeutic strategies. Several cellular therapies have subsequently been investigated, including chimeric antigen receptor (CAR)-T cells, T-cell receptor (TCR)-engineered T cells, and gamma delta (γδ) T-cell therapies. These approaches have shown encouraging activity in preclinical models; early clinical studies of CAR-T cells support the feasibility of locoregional delivery in pediatric central nervous system (CNS) tumors, although objective responses remain limited and MB-specific efficacy is unestablished. γδ T-cell and TCR-engineered approaches remain preclinical in MB. However, challenges including antigen heterogeneity, immune escape, limited immune-cell trafficking across the central nervous system barriers, and tumor microenvironment-mediated resistance remain major obstacles. This paper summarizes the current understanding of the MB immune microenvironment. It also discusses recent advances in immunotherapeutic strategies, particularly precision cellular therapies. Future strategies involve multi-omics profiling, cellular engineering, and adjustments to the tumor microenvironment. Individualized immunotherapy guided by tumor molecular identity and the immune ecosystem may offer a new approach to improving outcomes in children with high-risk MB.

title: CAR Macrophages in Brain Tumor Immunotherapy: Molecular Engineering Strategies and Emerging Frontiers.
authors: Ou H, Yun J, Han Y et al.
abstract: The CNS is partly shielded from immune attack, which allows tumor cells to escape many conventional therapies, including CAR-T. CAR-M therapy is an alternative approach that exploits the ability of myeloid cells to enter the CNS, engulf tumor cells, and shift the immunosuppressive microenvironment. This review focuses on molecular engineering principles for next-generation CAR-M constructs, including signaling domain selection, CD47-SIRPα checkpoint strategies, and gene delivery platforms for myeloid cells. We also discuss CNS-specific delivery routes and the multi-layered anti-tumor mechanisms of CAR-M, such as phagocytosis, TME remodeling, and innate-adaptive immune bridging. Combination strategies with checkpoint inhibitors, oncolytic viruses, and chemotherapy are analyzed, together with emerging approaches like SIGLEC9-based chimeric switch receptors, enucleated MSC-mediated in situ CAR-M generation, and circRNA-based CAR expression. We then address CNS-specific safety considerations and translational challenges.

title: EPHB4-Targeted CAR-T Cells Demonstrate Antitumor Activity in an Orthotopic Tongue PDX Model of Oral Squamous Cell Carcinoma.
authors: Kinjo M, Ohnuki K, Suzuki T et al.
abstract: Oral squamous cell carcinoma (OSCC) remains associated with poor outcomes and functional impairment despite multimodal treatment, underscoring the need for effective and less invasive therapeutic strategies. Ephrin type-B receptor 4 (EPHB4) is frequently expressed on OSCC cells and represents a potential target for chimeric antigen receptor (CAR)-T cell therapy. In this study, we evaluated the antitumor activity of EPHB4-targeted CAR-T cells (131CAR) using in vitro cytotoxicity assays against the OSCC cell line HSC-4 and an orthotopic tongue patient-derived xenograft (PDX) model established from an OSCC tumor (OC-15) in NOD scid gamma (NSG) mice. Flow cytometry confirmed EPHB4 expression in HSC-4 cells (~90%) and OC-15-derived tumor cells (~68%). In vitro assays demonstrated effector-to-target-ratio-dependent cytotoxicity of 131CAR against HSC-4 cells. In the main in vivo experiment, intratumoral administration of 131CAR suppressed tumor growth and significantly reduced the cytokeratin-defined carcinoma area compared with control groups. Digital pathology further showed a reduced proportion of EPHB4-positive area within the residual carcinoma and increased accumulation of human CD8+ cells in 131CAR-treated tumors. These findings indicate that EPHB4-targeted CAR-T cells exert antitumor activity in an orthotopic OSCC model and support further preclinical evaluation of this therapeutic approach in anatomically relevant settings.

title: Effective targeting of pediatric bone sarcoma cells by engineered CAR.HER2 T-cells.
authors: Aurigemma M, Quintarelli C, De Falco P et al.
abstract:
BACKGROUND: Pediatric and adolescent osteosarcoma (OS) and Ewing's sarcoma (EWS) are highly aggressive malignancies associated with poor outcomes in the relapsed or metastatic setting, where survival rates remain below 20-30% despite intensive multimodal therapy. The transmembrane tyrosine-kinase receptor HER2 is expressed in a substantial proportion of OS and EWS; however, current HER2-directed antibody-based therapies show limited efficacy, likely due to the low antigen expression in these tumors.
METHODS: HER2 expression was evaluated by flow-cytometry on adult and pediatric tumor cell lines, as well as in biopsy tissues from pediatric sarcoma patients. We generated two third-generation CAR.HER2 constructs carrying ΔCD19 as both a tracking marker and safety switch to improve the safety profile. Retroviral vectors, (4D5)CAR.HER2 and (2C4)CAR.HER2, incorporate trastuzumab- or pertuzumab-derived single-chain variable fragments (scFvs), respectively, which linker was optimized through structural bioinformatic. These scFvs are coupled to the CD28 and 4-1BB costimulatory domains and the CD3ζ signaling domains, to promote robust T-cell activation and persistence. The antitumor activity of CAR.HER2 T-cells was assessed in vitro and in vivo against HER2 + OS and EWS tumors.
RESULTS: HER2 expression was detected in 87% of tumor cell lines and in 38.5% of OS and 36.8% of EWS patient samples. Both CAR.HER2 T-cells exhibited strong CAR expression and comparable immunophenotypic profiles, following T-cell transduction. In 2D/3D in vitro models, CAR.HER2 T-cells showed potent cytotoxic activity against HER2-high OS and HER2-low EWS cells, including trastuzumab-deruxtecan (T-DXd)-resistant tumor cell lines. In in vivo models, both CAR.HER2 T-cells achieved complete regression in HER2-high OS xenografts, while in HER2-low EWS xenograft model only (4D5)CAR.HER2 T-cells induced full tumor eradication, whereas (2C4)CAR.HER2 T-cells delayed tumor progression without achieving full tumor elimination. Xenoreactivity associated with CAR.HER2 T-cell expansion was successfully controlled via ΔCD19 activation using an anti CD19/CD3 T-cell engager, enabling selective CAR T-cell depletion and toxicity resolution.
CONCLUSIONS: Overall, (4D5)CAR.HER2 T-cells demonstrated superior antitumor activity, persistence, and functional fitness, achieving rapid tumor clearance in HER2-low pediatric sarcoma models. The integrated ΔCD19 safety switch induce a prompt CAR T-cell elimination. These findings support the clinical translation of high-affinity-(4D5)CAR.HER2 T-cells and suggest broader applicability of this design for targeting HER2-low tumors and overcoming resistance to HER2-immunotherapy.

title: Combined BRAF and RAS inhibition overcomes acquired resistance in BRAF-mutated colorectal cancer
summary: BRAFV600E-mutated colorectal cancer is aggressive and associated with poor patient prognosis. Combined BRAF and EGFR inhibition improves patient outcomes but acquired resistance limits treatment efficacy. We integrated molecular profiling and functional drug screening of BRAF-mutated cell lines (n = 17) and patient-derived organoids (n = 17) to identify and target mechanisms of intrinsic and acquired resistance. Acquired resistance to dual BRAF and EGFR inhibition was associated with RAS activation, including emerging NRAS hotspot mutations, KRAS amplification and transcriptomic MAPK signaling. Intrinsic and acquired resistance shared transcriptomic features including IGF1R, PI3K, inflammatory, and proteasome-associated signaling. Screening of 28 drug combinations revealed context-dependent sensitivity to co-inhibition of BRAF with IGF1R, MEK and SRC. Notably, RAS inhibitors daraxonrasib and RMC-7977 showed pronounced synergy with encorafenib in models with acquired RAS alterations, restoring treatment sensitivity and suppressing ERK1/2 phosphorylation. These findings identify acquired resistance associated with RAS reactivation as a therapeutic vulnerability and provide a preclinical rationale for combined BRAF and RAS inhibition in BRAF-mutated colorectal cancer.

title: Discovery of Zoldonrasib (RMC-9805), a Potent and Orally Bioavailable RAS(ON) G12D-Selective, Covalent, Tri-Complex Inhibitor for the Treatment of Patients with RAS G12D-Addicted Cancers.
authors: Burnett GL, Weller C, Jiang L et al.
abstract: RAS mutations are among the most frequent oncogenic drivers in human cancer, and KRAS G12D is one of the most prevalent RAS alterations occurring in pancreatic ductal adenocarcinoma (PDAC), colorectal cancer (CRC), and non-small cell lung cancer. Here, we describe the structure-based SAR journey that led to the discovery of zoldonrasib (RMC-9805), an orally bioavailable RAS(ON) G12D-selective, covalent, tri-complex inhibitor. Discovery of an aziridine-2-carboxamide-based warhead and a rigid spirocyclic linker enabled selective covalent engagement of KRAS G12D in its active, GTP-bound state. Zoldonrasib exhibited potent inhibition of KRAS G12D signaling and proliferation in KRAS G12D-dependent cancer cells, favorable ADME and cross-species pharmacokinetic properties, and selectivity over RAS-independent cellular models. In vivo, zoldonrasib produced deep and durable suppression of tumor RAS pathway signaling and induced dose-dependent tumor regressions in KRAS G12D-driven xenograft models. Currently, zoldonrasib is in clinical evaluation for KRAS G12D mutant solid tumors.

title: Clinical and Molecular Associations of ITGB1 Expression in Lung Adenocarcinoma and Lung Squamous Cell Carcinoma: A TCGA-Based Study.
authors: Lee SH, Kim SG, An JH et al.
abstract: Background and Objectives: Integrin beta 1 (ITGB1) participates in cell-extracellular matrix signaling, but its associations with clinical outcomes and molecular features in non-small cell lung cancer (NSCLC) may vary by histological subtype. We reassessed its clinical and transcriptomic associations in TCGA lung adenocarcinoma (LUAD) and lung squamous cell carcinoma (LUSC), explicitly testing interaction effects and microenvironmental confounding. Materials and Methods: Primary-tumor RNA-sequencing profiles from 492 LUAD and 488 LUSC patients were linked to standardized TCGA Clinical Data Resource outcomes. We performed median-based Kaplan-Meier analysis; Cox models of continuous ITGB1 expression per within-subtype standard deviation, with stage-stratified clinical adjustment; a common nine-gene expression correlation panel; ESTIMATE-score sensitivity analyses; tumor DNA mutation/copy-number comparisons; and phenotype-permutation Hallmark gene set enrichment analysis (GSEA). Results: After clinical and stromal/immune score adjustment, elevated ITGB1 expression was significantly associated with poor overall survival in LUAD (hazard ratio [HR] = 1.357, 95% confidence interval [CI]: 1.145-1.610) and favorable overall survival in LUSC (HR = 0.741, 95% CI: 0.627-0.876). Higher ITGB1 expression was also associated with PFI in LUAD (HR 1.240) and LUSC (HR 1.333), but survival interaction by histology was not significant (OS p = 0.198; PFI p = 0.724). ITGB1 correlations with KRAS and PIK3CA were stronger in LUAD than LUSC even after microenvironmental adjustment. SOX2 and PIK3CA amplification showed significant histology interactions with ITGB1 expression (adjusted interaction β = -0.651 and -0.613). Gene set enrichment analysis (GSEA) revealed within-cohort enrichment patterns associated with ITGB1 expression, highlighting pathways such as EMT, angiogenesis, and coagulation in LUAD, whereas MYC Targets, E2F Targets, and DNA Repair were enriched in LUSC. These findings represent within-cohort enrichment patterns and do not establish statistically significant differences between histologies. Conclusions: ITGB1 exhibits histology-associated molecular and microenvironmental patterns, without convincing evidence of differing survival hazard ratios between LUAD and LUSC. These retrospective findings require independent and functional validation.

title: KRAS Inhibitor Resistance in Lung Cancer: Mechanisms and Therapeutic Opportunities.
authors: Garza SG, Kundu ST, Gibbons DL
abstract:
BACKGROUND/OBJECTIVES: Resistance to currently available KRAS inhibitors presents a major therapeutic challenge in non-small cell lung cancer (NSCLC). The purpose of this review is to describe the various mechanisms of resistance to KRAS inhibitors, including the activation of an epithelial-to-mesenchymal transition (EMT) program, tumor microenvironment modulation, and the rewiring of KRAS-addicted cancer cells towards other signaling pathways that promote growth and proliferation amidst KRAS inhibition.
RESULTS: Through a narrative review of recent and landmark studies in the field of KRAS inhibitor resistance, we summarize the primary non-genetic mechanisms of resistance to KRAS inhibitors as follows: receptor tyrosine kinase-mediated induction of both wild-type and mutant KRAS and the activation of several bypass signaling pathways, such as PI3K/AKT, Gas6/AXL, and YAP/TEAD/Hippo.
CONCLUSIONS: We conclude that no single non-genetic driver of resistance is responsible for all cases of KRAS inhibitor resistance; rather, effective therapeutic strategies may also be informed by the tumor co-mutational status and the transcriptional phenotype of the tumor, including a mesenchymal or highly plastic cell state.

title: Ki-67 Across Human Cancers: A Narrative Review of Its Prognostic Significance and Challenges in Standardization.
authors: Atout M, Mahmoud M, Garatli T et al.
abstract: Background/Objectives: Ki-67 is a cell proliferation marker which is tightly coupled to the cell cycle. Its importance stems from the information it provides on prognosis, response to therapy, and clinical outcomes in several tumors. However, several gaps regarding its use should be addressed before it can be used as a standard-of-care test in cancer management. Methods: A structured literature search of articles was conducted using PubMed to evaluate Ki-67 for its prognostic value across human cancers. The primary areas of interest were immunohistochemistry (IHC) methods, the impact of Ki-67 index variability on clinical judgment, and the potential for standardizing evaluation provided by AI-powered tools and automated digital image analysis (DIA). Results: In different cancers, Ki-67 overexpression is related to worse clinicopathological characteristics, shorter overall survival, and higher tumor burden. Increased Ki-67 expression in breast cancer was associated with higher risk of recurrence in the ER-positive, HER2-negative subtypes. Similarly, in prostate cancer, higher Ki-67 scores correlated well with higher Gleason scores and early biochemical relapse. In lung cancer, Ki-67 levels were found to be higher in the later stages, in metastatic disease, and in patients with poor survival. However, the cut-off values varied widely (5-50%). Conclusions: The Ki-67 index is a promising biomarker, which, with some refinements, may prove to be an invaluable tool in the management of malignant tumors. Future studies should therefore be directed towards reducing variability by increasing standardization and establishing standardized, tumor-specific cut-off values.

title: Macropinocytosis in KRAS-Mutant Cancers: Biological Functions and Therapeutic Opportunities in Pancreatic Ductal Adenocarcinoma.
authors: Yu JR, Yu XY, Wen KL et al.
abstract: Oncogenic mutations in KRAS are primary drivers of human malignancies, particularly in pancreatic, colorectal, and lung adenocarcinomas. Although allele-selective inhibitors have shown clinical activity in some settings, their applicability varies by KRAS allele and tumor type. An important metabolic adaptation observed in selected KRAS-mutant tumor models, particularly pancreatic ductal adenocarcinoma (PDAC), is increased macropinocytosis, a clathrin-independent endocytic process that enables the nonselective engulfment of extracellular fluids and their solutes to support tumor growth. Although this process is physiologically restricted in most quiescent cells, macropinocytosis enables extracellular protein scavenging in several KRAS-mutant tumor models, thereby supporting amino acid availability and metabolism under nutrient-limited conditions. Macropinocytosis-associated uptake of cholesterol and ATP has also been reported in selected breast/ovarian and A549 lung cancer models, respectively; however, lipid acquisition through this route has not been established in KRAS-mutant PDAC, and the dependence of ATP uptake on mutant KRAS remains unclear. Beyond nutrient acquisition, macropinocytosis can mitigate microenvironmental stress, contribute to cytoskeletal remodeling and invasive progression, and reduce treatment sensitivity in selected preclinical models, although these effects depend on tumor lineage, genetic background, and experimental conditions. These context-dependent adaptive functions make hyperactive macropinocytic flux a potential gateway for targeted intervention. Therapeutic strategies currently under investigation include inhibition of macropinocytic nutrient uptake, utilization of macropinocytosis for drug delivery, and induction of methuosis, a non-apoptotic death phenotype associated with extensive vacuolization. Most evidence remains preclinical. This review systematically elucidates the molecular mechanisms governing macropinocytosis, its pleiotropic roles in tumor survival and malignant progression, with emphasis on PDAC, and discusses the evidence and limitations relevant to therapeutic development.

title: Metabolic profiling of adaptive responses and functional determinants of Sotorasib sensitivity in KRASG12C mutant NSCLC.
authors: Lee C, An YJ, Choi DH et al.
abstract: Despite the clinical success of Sotorasib in KRASG12C mutant non-small cell lung cancer (NSCLC), drug resistance remains a major challenge. While genomic mechanisms of resistance have been studied extensively, the metabolic adaptations accompanying survival under KRASG12C inhibition are poorly understood. This study aimed to delineate the time-dependent metabolic trajectories of KRASG12C mutant NSCLC cells under Sotorasib and to determine how a resistant (H23) and a sensitive (H358) cell line diverge. Untargeted metabolomics, combined with measurements of glutathione peroxidase 4 (GPX4), reactive oxygen species (ROS), and lipid peroxidation, was performed after treatment with 1 μM Sotorasib for 6, 48, and 72 h. Both cell lines exhibited a conserved biphasic metabolic response, in which the pyrimidine nucleoside triphosphates and glutathione-related metabolites remained high at 6 h, while glycine, serine, L-kynurenine, and nicotinamide accumulated during the late phase (48 and 72 h). Although the adenylate energy charge and reduced glutathione declined in both cell lines, their redox fates diverged. In H23 cells, lipid peroxidation increased only to approximately 150% of the control level, despite declining GPX4 protein and an increasing NADP+/NADPH ratio. Conversely, H358 cells maintained GPX4 protein but showed lipid peroxidation of 260%, a cMYC mRNA rebound of 1.6-fold, and a fall of the total ROS signal to 15% as viable cells were lost. Our findings indicate that the extent of lipid peroxidation, rather than the abundance of GPX4 protein, is associated with the divergent Sotorasib responses of these lines, and they nominate late-phase glutathione metabolism as a candidate target for combination with Sotorasib.

title: Integrated tissue and longitudinal ctDNA profiling reveal distinct genomic evolutionary trajectories associated with response to first-line immunotherapy and chemioimmunotherapy in advanced NSCLC patients.
authors: Nicoś M, Galant N, Krzyżanowska N et al.
abstract:
BACKGROUND: Immune checkpoint inhibitors (ICIs) have become a central component of first-line treatment in advanced non-small cell lung cancer (NSCLC). Despite the implementation of predictive biomarkers such as PD-L1 expression on tumor cells, treatment response remains highly heterogeneous, and the mechanisms underlying durable clinical benefit and the evolution of therapy resistance are still poorly understood.
METHODS: We performed integrated longitudinal genomic profiling of 520 tumor tissue and liquid biopsy samples collected from 127 patients with advanced NSCLC treated with first-line pembrolizumab-based therapy. Low-pass whole-genome sequencing (lp-WGS) and targeted sequencing were used to characterize copy number alteration (CNA) dynamics, mutational processes, and clonal evolution associated with treatment response. Longitudinal circulating tumor DNA (ctDNA) analyses were integrated with baseline tumor tissue profiling to compare genomic trajectories between short- and long-responders.
RESULTS: Both short- and long-responders initially demonstrated transient molecular response characterized by broad CNA normalization and reduction of detectable variants during the first months of treatment. However, longitudinal analyses revealed major differences in evolutionary dynamics between response groups. Short responders showed early shifts in subclonal architecture and expansion of resistant clonal populations, whereas long responders maintained relative evolutionary stability, with delayed diversification during therapy. Recurrent focal CNAs associated with therapy resistance included persistent amplification of the 3q22-q28 region harboring multiple oncogenic drivers, as well as alterations involving FGFR1, MYC, CCNE1, CDKN2A/B, and ICOSLG loci. Mutational analyses revealed enrichment of KRAS/STK11/KEAP1 alterations and DNA repair deficiency-associated mutational signatures in short responders, whereas long responders showed enrichment of APOBEC-associated mutagenesis and ZFHX3 alterations. Longitudinal TP53 variant allele frequency (VAF) dynamics further demonstrated persistent clonal turnover in short responders compared with a marked reduction of TP53-mutant burden in long responders.
CONCLUSIONS: Our findings indicate that immunotherapy response in advanced NSCLC is shaped not only by baseline molecular characteristics but also by distinct evolutionary trajectories under treatment pressure. Longitudinal ctDNA profiling enables dynamic monitoring of genomic changes associated with resistant disease and may support improved stratification of patients receiving immunotherapy.

title: Smoking History and Clinical Heterogeneity in Small-Cell Lung Cancer: Survival and Treatment-Associated Outcomes in a Multicenter Cohort.
authors: Sun J, Wang T, Tian J et al.
abstract: Clinical and prognostic differences between never-smokers and ever-smokers with small-cell lung cancer (SCLC) remain incompletely characterized. We conducted a multicenter retrospective cohort study to compare clinical characteristics and survival outcomes between never-smokers and ever-smokers with SCLC, evaluate potential indirect pathways linking smoking history with overall survival (OS), and explore treatment-associated survival patterns. A total of 1153 patients from three tertiary hospitals in China were included, comprising 340 never-smokers and 813 ever-smokers. Ever-smoking was associated with worse OS in univariable analysis (HR = 1.20, 95% CI: 1.04-1.38; p = 0.013), but this association was attenuated after multivariable adjustment (HR = 1.04, 95% CI: 0.82-1.32; p = 0.729). In separate single-mediator analyses, indirect effects were observed through surgical resection and clinical stage, with estimated mediated proportions of 39.9% and 16.1%, respectively; these estimates were derived from separate models and are not additive. Exploratory analyses of recorded treatment history showed chemotherapy-associated lower mortality hazards in both smoking groups, while ever-smoking was associated with poorer OS among patients with recorded radiotherapy exposure. Because exact treatment timing was unavailable, these treatment-related findings should be interpreted as exploratory associations rather than causal treatment effects. Smoking history was associated with distinct clinical characteristics but was not independently associated with survival after multivariable adjustment. These findings support further prospective investigation of smoking-associated clinical heterogeneity in SCLC.

title: Composite Risk Scores Combining PET Metabolic Tumor Burden and Systemic Inflammation Stratify Survival in Patients with Extensive-Stage Small-Cell Lung Cancer Receiving Chemoimmunotherapy.
authors: Özçelik H, Mıldanoğlu MM, Güner AL et al.
abstract: Background and Objectives: Extensive-stage small-cell lung cancer (ES-SCLC) is an aggressive disease, and the survival benefit of adding immune checkpoint inhibitors (ICIs) to first-line chemotherapy is modest and heterogeneous; simple, accessible prognostic markers are therefore needed. We evaluated composite risk scores combining pretreatment positron emission tomography (PET)-derived metabolic tumor burden with systemic inflammatory markers in this setting. Materials and Methods: This single-center retrospective cohort study included 112 consecutive patients diagnosed between January 2019 and December 2025. Metabolic tumor volume (MTV) and total lesion glycolysis (TLG) on pretreatment 18F-fluorodeoxyglucose PET/computed tomography were combined with one of three blood-based inflammatory markers: neutrophil-to-lymphocyte ratio (NLR), platelet-to-lymphocyte ratio (PLR) or systemic immune-inflammation index (SII). Each component was scored 0 or 1 at the cohort median, yielding three risk scores of 0-3 points (RS1, NLR-based; RS2, PLR-based; RS3, SII-based) and low-, intermediate- and high-risk groups. Progression-free survival (PFS) and overall survival (OS) were analyzed with the Kaplan-Meier method, the log-rank test and separate multivariable Cox models for each score adjusted for performance status and liver and bone metastases; incremental value was assessed with Harrell's concordance index (C-index). Results: Median PFS was 7.70 months and median OS was 14.43 months, with a median follow-up of 27.6 months. All three scores stratified PFS and OS in univariable analysis (RS1: p = 0.008 and p = 0.002, respectively). RS1 was the only score independently associated with both outcomes (PFS: hazard ratio [HR] per risk tier 1.39, 95% confidence interval [CI] 1.04-1.86, p = 0.026; OS: HR 1.53, 95% CI 1.09-2.16, p = 0.014). RS2 and RS3 were not independently significant. RS1 modestly improved the C-index of clinical factors (by approximately 0.02), but NLR added no significant information beyond metabolic burden. Conclusions: A composite score combining PET-derived metabolic burden with NLR was independently associated with survival in ES-SCLC treated with chemoimmunotherapy, but its added discrimination was modest and driven mainly by the metabolic component; these exploratory findings require prospective validation.

title: Survival from Diagnosis Early Mortality and Recorded Systemic Therapy Lines in a Turkish Small Cell Lung Cancer Analytic Cohort.
authors: Kesen O, Çelik A
abstract: Background/Objectives: We described survival from diagnosis, early mortality, and recorded systemic therapy lines and explored the association between baseline brain metastases and mortality in a Turkish small cell lung cancer (SCLC) cohort. Methods: This retrospective single-center study included 131 eligible adults. Observed diagnoses ranged from 12 August 2009 to 23 May 2023. All included patients had died by follow-up ascertainment. Additional brain-metastasis analyses and calendar-period comparisons were exploratory and post hoc. Treatment calendar details, immunotherapy exposure, and cranial radiotherapy details were unavailable. Results: Median overall survival (OS) was 10.41 months (95% confidence interval [CI], 8.74-13.04); 30- and 90-day mortality were 5.3% and 12.2%. First-line platinum-etoposide was recorded in 99 patients (75.6%). Of 22 limited-stage patients, 21 received concurrent thoracic chemoradiotherapy with curative intent; one patient could not start anticancer therapy after pneumonia and rapid clinical deterioration. Within extensive-stage disease, the unadjusted brain-metastasis hazard ratio (HR) was 1.67 (95% CI, 0.98-2.86; p = 0.061), the log-rank p value was 0.059, and the adjusted HR was 1.98 (95% CI, 1.07-3.66; p = 0.029). A 5000-replicate bootstrap gave a percentile 95% CI of 1.10-4.87 and a bias-corrected and accelerated (BCa) 95% CI of 0.84-3.79. The original full-cohort brain-metastasis p value was 0.033 and became 0.099 after Bonferroni or Holm adjustment across three baseline findings. Conclusions: The analyses suggested a possible association between baseline brain metastases and higher mortality, but the original full-cohort association did not meet the significance threshold after Holm correction. Sparse exposure and unmeasured confounding make this finding hypothesis-generating. Clinic-based referral selection may limit generalizability.

title: From Cellular Plasticity to Relapse Competence in Small Cell Lung Cancer: Rethinking the Biology of Recurrence.
authors: Gara SK, Singh A
abstract: Small cell lung cancer (SCLC) is characterized by profound initial treatment sensitivity followed by frequent recurrence. Although genetic resistance contributes to disease progression, increasing evidence indicates that SCLC cells can transition among phenotypic states, allowing tumor composition and therapeutic vulnerabilities to evolve during treatment. How cellular plasticity and stem-like properties intersect with treatment persistence and subsequent tumor regeneration, however, remains poorly understood. In this Review, we integrate evidence from SCLC developmental biology, cancer stemness, cellular plasticity, and longitudinal tumor evolution to examine the transition from treatment response to recurrence. We distinguish treatment persistence from relapse competence, defined here as the functional capacity of therapy-surviving cells to regenerate recurrent tumor growth rather than as a discrete cellular subtype. We discuss how genetic selection and non-genetic adaptation shape residual disease, how cell state evolution alters therapeutic vulnerabilities, and how lineage-aware experimental approaches could identify recurrence-driving populations. Understanding the cellular trajectories connecting treatment-naive, residual, and recurrent SCLC may reveal opportunities to therapeutically intercept the evolutionary processes that enable recurrence.

title: Silent but Aggressive: A Case of Cervical Large-Cell Neuroendocrine Carcinoma with Repeatedly Normal Cytology in a 22-Year-Old Postpartum Patient.
authors: Groza DM, Nicula RL, Oancea MD et al.
abstract: Background/Objectives: Neuroendocrine carcinoma of the cervix (NECC) is a rare, aggressive variant of cervical cancer (approximately 1-1.5% of cases), and large-cell neuroendocrine carcinoma (LCNEC) is an even rarer subtype. Diagnosis is often delayed because symptoms are non-specific and cytology may fail to detect the disease. We report this case to highlight the diagnostic challenge posed by LCNEC in a young patient with repeatedly normal cytology. Methods: We describe the diagnostic work-up and multimodal management of a 22-year-old woman who presented with post-coital bleeding nine months after her second full-term vaginal delivery. Results: Two Babeș-Papanicolaou smears obtained three months apart were negative for intraepithelial lesion or malignancy. Persistent bleeding prompted a loop electrosurgical excision procedure (LEEP), which revealed a poorly differentiated (high-grade) LCNEC. Clinical examination and MRI showed proximal parametrial involvement and a left external iliac lymph node metastasis (FIGO 2018 stage IIIC1r, cT2bN1M0). The patient received definitive chemoradiotherapy (external beam radiotherapy with a simultaneous integrated boost and high-dose-rate brachytherapy) with six cycles of platinum-etoposide chemotherapy (two concurrent, four adjuvant), achieving a complete response with no evidence of disease approximately three years after treatment. Conclusions: This report illustrates that cytology can be repeatedly negative in NECC and that persistent symptoms or a visible cervical lesion warrant histological evaluation. Given its aggressive clinical course, LCNEC requires the rapid initiation of combined local and systemic therapy.

title: Report-Defined FDG-PET/CT Positivity Is Common Across the Clinical Spectrum of Well-Differentiated Pulmonary Neuroendocrine Tumors.
authors: Muzykovskaia E, Fraenkel M, Twito O
abstract: Background/Objectives: The clinical significance of 18F-fluorodeoxyglucose (FDG) uptake in well-differentiated pulmonary neuroendocrine tumors (WD-PulNETs) remains uncertain. We assessed the prevalence of FDG positivity in routine clinical practice. Methods: This multicenter retrospective cohort included histologically confirmed typical or atypical pulmonary carcinoids. FDG PET/CT was classified as positive or negative according to the original nuclear-medicine report. Results: Of 91 WD-PulNETs patients, 81 had sufficient data for analysis. The cohort included 67 patients (82.7%) with typical carcinoids and 14 (17.3%) with atypical carcinoids. FDG PET/CT was performed in 50 patients (61.7%), of whom 46 (92.0%; 95% CI, 81.2-96.8%) had report-defined FDG positivity in the primary pulmonary tumor. FDG positivity was observed in 39 of 42 patients (92.9%) with typical carcinoids and 7 of 8 (87.5%) with atypical carcinoids. Comparisons between patients who underwent FDG PET/CT and those who did not revealed no statistically significant differences in most evaluated clinicopathological characteristics. However, somatostatin analogue treatment was more frequent among patients who underwent FDG PET/CT (35.6% vs. 7.7%; p = 0.011). Conclusion: Report-defined FDG positivity was highly prevalent across the spectrum of WD-PulNETs, including typical carcinoids. Potential selection bias and the small number of patients preclude firm conclusions about its discriminatory or prognostic significance.

title: Effectiveness and safety of consolidation PD-L1 inhibitor therapy after chemoradiotherapy in non-progressive limited-stage small cell lung cancer: a multicenter real-world study.
authors: Zhu J, Li M, Xu J et al.
abstract:
BACKGROUND: The real-world effectiveness and safety of consolidation immune checkpoint inhibitors (ICIs) for limited-stage small-cell lung cancer (LS-SCLC) remain unclear. This study aimed to evaluate the real-world outcomes of this approach.
MATERIALS AND METHODS: We retrospectively evaluated patients with LS-SCLC who received definitive chemoradiotherapy (CRT) at two institutions between January 2022 and January 2025. They were grouped by receipt of consolidation immunotherapy (programmed death-ligand 1 [PD-L1] inhibitor) and propensity score matched (1:2). The primary outcome measures were progression-free survival (PFS) and overall survival (OS); the secondary outcome measures were brain metastasis-free survival (BMFS), intrathoracic and extrathoracic PFS, and safety.
RESULTS: 211 matched patients were evaluated (non-consolidation immunotherapy, 140; consolidation immunotherapy, 71). The median follow-up was 34.7 months. Consolidation immunotherapy was associated with longer PFS (18.9 vs. 12.1 months; p = 0.026), OS (not reached vs. 31.6 months; p < 0.001), intrathoracic and extrathoracic PFS (p = 0.025 and 0.006) and was an independent prognostic factor for PFS and OS. In exploratory analyses stratified by best response to CRT, consolidation immunotherapy was associated with longer OS in the PR subgroup, but no statistically significant treatment-by-response interaction was observed for either OS or PFS. In the consolidation immunotherapy group, OS was similar across initiation intervals, whereas PFS was most favorable when PD-L1 inhibitors were initiated 4-6 weeks after CRT. Prophylactic cranial irradiation (PCI) was associated with longer BMFS; safety was comparable between groups.
CONCLUSION: Consolidation PD-L1 inhibition after definitive CRT was associated with improved survival and disease control with manageable safety in real-world patients with LS-SCLC.

title: From Drug Toxicity to System Failure: A FAIR-Swiss Cheese Framework for Model-Based Allocation of Excess Risk in Immune Checkpoint Inhibitor-Related Adverse Events.
authors: Ellenberg E, Yaacov A, Katorza E et al.
abstract: Background/Objectives: Severe immune-related adverse events (irAEs) after immune checkpoint inhibitor therapy can reflect drug toxicity, patient susceptibility and the performance of care processes. We propose and demonstrate a transparent method for allocating modelled excess risk among these factors, using pembrolizumab-based treatment of non-small cell lung cancer (NSCLC) as the motivating setting. Methods: The framework combines FAIR methodology (filtering evidence, association quantification, individual partitioning, reasoned interpretation) with a Swiss cheese model of seven sequential care barriers. Stage 1 allocates excess irAE incidence among biological factors. Stage 2 allocates excess risk of progression to severe harm after irAE onset among a biological progression factor and individual care-barrier failures. Both stages use exact Shapley values of an explicit risk model with a defined reference state. Published estimates and assumptions are separated in a parameter table; deterministic, structural and Monte Carlo sensitivity analyses and two published case reports illustrate the method. Results: In Stage 1, conditional on using the pooled 16% pneumonitis incidence as the risk without interstitial lung disease, pembrolizumab received 34.8% and pre-existing interstitial lung disease 65.2% of the modelled excess pneumonitis risk. In a synthetic Stage 2 example with two assumed care failures, the barriers received 69.4% of the modelled excess progression risk, whereas repairing both failures reduced modelled risk by 80.0%. The system share ranged from 54.2% to 78.8% across assumed biological multipliers and from 66.7% to 71.4% across link functions, factor grouping and pathway dependence. At realistic baseline risks, multiplying several barrier effects produced probabilities above 1. Within the assumed ranges, monitoring made the largest contribution in only 3.4% of simulations. Conclusions: The framework makes the allocation of modelled excess risk explicit and reproducible. Its outputs are allocations under stated assumptions, not estimates of individual causation, preventability or legal responsibility, and require empirical parameterisation and validation before clinical or medico-legal use.

title: The Role of Smoking History in the Efficacy of Neoadjuvant and Perioperative Therapy for Lung Cancer.
authors: Gargapati AS, Nixon K, Massarelli E
abstract: Lung cancer is one of the leading causes of cancer-related mortality worldwide, and neoadjuvant therapy has become a cornerstone in the management of resectable non-small-cell lung cancer (NSCLC). Growing evidence suggests that smoking history is an important clinical and biological factor that influences response to neoadjuvant treatment. This review synthesizes epidemiologic, translational, and clinical evidence, including findings from landmark clinical trials. It aims to evaluate the efficacy of neoadjuvant chemotherapy, immunotherapy, targeted therapy, and multimodal treatment strategies according to smoking status. Furthermore, this review examines the molecular and immunologic mechanisms underlying the differential treatment responses observed among current, former, and never-smokers. Ultimately, there is an increasing need to conduct prospective smoking-stratified studies and integrate smoking history into medical practice to develop more personalized neoadjuvant therapies for patients with lung cancer.

title: Early Detection of Lung Cancer: Lessons From Major Screening Trials.
authors: Alam A
abstract: Lung cancer is the top-ranked cancer both in terms of incidence and mortality worldwide. The disease generally exhibits poor prognosis and 5-year survival owing to late diagnosis. Long-term tobacco smoking is the leading risk factor for lung cancer. Population-based screening of long-term smokers can facilitate early detection and improve treatment outcomes and survival. Clinical trials using various diagnostic tools have been carried out for lung cancer screening. Trials with chest X-ray and sputum cytology, alone or in combination, did not offer any mortality benefit, whereas low-dose computed tomography (LDCT) showed significant reduction in mortality in 2 large trials, the National Lung Screening Trial (NLST) and the Dutch-Belgian Lung Cancer Screening Trial (NELSON trial). Based on NLST results, the United States Preventive Services Task Force (USPSTF) established the eligibility criteria for lung cancer screening in the United States. Because lung cancer cases also occur in nonsmokers and a significant proportion of smokers were ineligible for screening with USPSTF criteria, risk prediction tools including risk factors other than age and smoking history for inclusion of such populations are being validated. In addition, the majority of the nodules detected by LDCT are benign and lack manifestations specific to lung cancer. Lung cancer-specific biomarkers for detection are being validated to select individuals at higher risk for LDCT screening and to supplement LDCT to reduce false positives. This review aims to provide an overview of landmark clinical trials for lung cancer screening and the lessons learned from them for population-based lung cancer screening.

title: An integrated overview from RadoNorm work package 4: advances and remaining challenges in radon and NORM risk assessment.
authors: Nieminen V, Aamodt G, Aarsand AS et al.
abstract: This paper synthesizes the achievements of Work Package 4 (WP4) of the European RadoNorm project (2020-2025) in radon and naturally occurring radioactive material (NORM) risk assessment. WP4 addressed four interconnected questions: the joint action of radon and tobacco smoke in lung carcinogenesis, health effects beyond adult lung cancer such as extrapulmonary diseases and childhood cancers, methodological uncertainties in radon risk estimates, also including thoron interference, and combined radiological and chemical stressors in wildlife.Combining epidemiological, mechanistic, dosimetric, and ecological approaches, the project advanced understanding on several fronts. On the epidemiological side, re-analysis of three European case-control studies indicated that the radon-smoking interaction was better described as sub-multiplicative than strictly multiplicative, with the functional form varying between populations. Lifetime Excess Absolute Risk estimates were in turn found to depend on model choice, with miner-based models yielding higher values per exposure unit than residential-based ones. A multinational childhood cancer analysis used organ-specific radon doses for the first time, whereas investigations of extrapulmonary endpoints found no clear evidence of radon-related risks at low exposures, however uncertainties remain. Mechanistic work complemented these findings by identifying conserved alterations in DNA repair pathways across species and distinct molecular profiles from combined radon and cigarette smoke exposure, with Adverse Outcome Pathway and Aggregate Exposure Pathway frameworks providing a mechanistic basis for the combined effects. Methodological and ecological contributions complemented the results: historical radon surveys in low-radon regions were shown to overestimate radon concentrations by up to a factor of two when thoron contributions were ignored, and a new population-level model incorporating mortality, reproduction, repair, and acclimation processes extended risk assessment to combined radiological and chemical stressors in non-human biota.Building on these results, six research directions are proposed to guide the next generation of work in this field. On the mechanistic and biological side, these include the translation of qualitative mechanistic evidence into quantitative Adverse Outcome Pathways that link defined exposure levels to adverse outcomes, a broader characterization of low-dose non-cancer and developmental effects at environmentally relevant exposure levels, and the derivation of age-specific exposure-response functions to inform radiation protection guidance for children. On the measurement and infrastructure side, systematic quantification of thoron-related bias at the European scale through coordinated detector re-evaluation and paired radon-thoron measurement campaigns, together with the deployment of federated analysis platforms to enable multinational pooled analyses, would support the empirical basis of future risk estimates. In the ecological domain, empirical parameterization of population models for chronic low-dose mixed exposures is required to render such models predictive rather than exploratory. Addressing these research directions would contribute to keeping regulatory frameworks aligned with the EU Beating Cancer Plan and One Health strategies informed by current scientific evidence.

title: Associations of early tobacco exposure and smoking dose with all-cause and cause-specific cancer risk: A prospective cohort study.
authors: Liu W, Su BW, Hou JY et al.
abstract:
INTRODUCTION: The long-term association of early tobacco exposure with adult cancer risk remains uncertain, and dose-response associations between cigarette smoking and cancer may be nonlinear.
METHODS: We analyzed prospective UK Biobank data through 1 July 2023. All-cause analyses included 467333 participants for pack-years of smoking (PYS) and PYS/(recruitment age - 16) (PYSP), 402849 for maternal smoking during pregnancy (MSDP), and 404584 for age at smoking initiation (ASI). The primary ASI analysis used self-reported never smokers as the reference and excluded ever smokers without initiation age and discordant never smokers with recorded initiation age. Cox models estimated hazard ratios (HRs) with demographic (Model 1) and extended (Model 2) adjustment; ASI Model 2 omitted smoking status. ASI trends were tested among initiators only. Four-knot restricted cubic splines examined exploratory dose-response patterns.
RESULTS: In the primary ASI cohort, median follow-up was 14.11 years, with 5263895 person-years, 1037 participants censored at loss to follow-up, and 60160 recorded all-cause cancer events. Compared with never smoking, ASI Model 2 hours were 1.11 (95% CI: 1.09-1.14) for adult, 1.16 (95% CI: 1.13-1.18) for adolescent, and 1.24 (95% CI: 1.15-1.35) for childhood initiation. The initiator-only all-cause trend had nominal p=0.004 and false discovery rate (FDR)=0.038; oropharyngeal cancer showed no corresponding trend (p=0.693). MSDP was associated with all-cause cancer (HR=1.05; 95% CI: 1.03-1.07). Each standard-deviation increase in PYS and PYSP was associated with all-cause cancer (both HR=1.06; 95% CI: 1.05-1.07). Spline analyses indicated nonlinear associations of both dose measures with all-cause and lung cancer (nominal p for nonlinearity ≤0.0013).
CONCLUSIONS: These observational associations support continued evaluation of early tobacco exposure and cumulative smoking dose as cancer-risk markers. Comparisons with never smoking and initiation-age trends among smokers address different questions. The results do not establish causal effects or demonstrate the benefit of a specific preventive intervention.

title: LPNScreen: a longitudinal pulmonary nodule malignancy risk prediction model based on temporal interval and feature evolution modeling.
authors: Wang M, Li X, Feng M et al.
abstract:
INTRODUCTION: Longitudinal CT provides valuable information for assessing pulmonary nodule malignancy risk and may improve access to lung cancer screening and follow-up care in resource-constrained primary-care settings. However, single-time-point CT-based methods cannot fully exploit temporal evolution across serial examinations, while the limited computational resources available in primary care also hinder the deployment of large-scale models.
METHODS: To address these challenges, we propose LPNScreen, a lightweight longitudinal framework for pulmonary nodule malignancy prediction. LPNScreen consists of three complementary components: centercontext spatial attention, which enhances discriminative nodule and surrounding contextual representations; interval-aware temporal modeling, which incorporates actual follow-up intervals to characterize irregular temporal dependencies; and tri-pair change modeling, which explicitly captures both adjacent and long-range nodule evolution across longitudinal scans.
RESULTS: Experimental results showed that LPNScreen achieved AUCs of 82.13% and 94.11% on the NLSTLPN and DMULPN datasets, respectively. Extensive comparative experiments and ablation studies further demonstrated the effectiveness of the proposed framework and its robustness across datasets with different follow-up patterns. In addition, computational complexity analysis confirmed the lightweight nature of LPNScreen, which requires only 0.434M parameters and 0.577G FLOPs.

title: Simultaneous Serum Profiling of Oxidative Stress, Inflammation, Hypoxia, and Angiogenesis Markers in Lung Cancer: Associations with Clinical Features and Survival.
authors: Serilmez M, Sen S, Özkan BN et al.
abstract: Lung cancer pathogenesis involves interconnected pathways, including oxidative stress, inflammation, and hypoxia-induced angiogenesis. This exploratory pilot study aimed to profile serum biomarkers related to these axes in individuals with lung cancer and healthy controls and to evaluate their interrelationships, clinicopathological associations and prognostic relevance. Archived serum samples from 74 individuals with lung cancer and 30 healthy never-smoking controls were analyzed for total oxidant status (TOS), total antioxidant status (TAS), oxidative stress index (OSI), 8-hydroxy-2'-deoxyguanosine (8-OHdG), ischemia-modified albumin (IMA), interleukin-1β (IL-1β), interleukin-6 (IL-6), tumor necrosis factor-α (TNF-α), hypoxia-inducible factor 1-α (HIF-1α), and vascular endothelial growth factor A (VEGF-A). Individuals with lung cancer had higher TOS, OSI, 8-OHdG, IMA, IL-1β, IL-6, TNF-α, HIF-1α and VEGF-A and lower TAS levels than controls (all p < 0.001). Because samples from the two groups were assayed on separate plates, these differences may partly reflect analytical batch effects and were not interpreted as diagnostic accuracy. Within the lung cancer group, oxidative stress indices showed weak correlations with IL-1β and HIF-1α that did not remain significant after correction for multiple testing. In multivariable Cox regression, ECOG performance status (HR 3.62), stage (HR 5.16) and distant metastasis (HR 3.18) were independently associated with overall survival. Higher VEGF-A levels were associated with longer survival (univariable HR 0.36, p = 0.015; HR 0.39, p = 0.048 after adjustment for histology, stage and ECOG), but this association was partly explained by histological subtype, was not significant in non-small cell lung cancer and did not survive correction for multiple testing; none of the other biomarkers was associated with survival. These findings indicate concurrent alterations of oxidative stress, inflammatory and hypoxia/angiogenesis markers in lung cancer and warrant validation in larger prospective cohorts with clinically relevant controls and all samples assayed together.

title: Second Primary Lung Cancer in Patients with Laryngeal Squamous Cell Carcinoma: A Retrospective Cohort Study.
authors: Šuljić N, Durdov T, Bubić T et al.
abstract: Patients with laryngeal squamous cell carcinoma (LSCC) often develop other malignancies, most commonly second primary lung cancer (SPLC). This study aimed to estimate the incidence of SPLC in LSCC patients and evaluate whether pulmonary nodules on baseline thoracic computed tomography (CT) predict SPLC development. In this single-center retrospective cohort study, 243 patients with LSCC diagnosed from 2017 to 2024 at the University Hospital of Split, Croatia, were followed, of whom 26 (10.7%) developed SPLC. The median time from LSCC to SPLC diagnosis was approximately 1.2 years. Patients with LSCC had an approximately eightfold higher risk of developing an SPLC than the general population (standardized incidence ratio [SIR] 8.40; 95% confidence interval [CI] 5.48-12.30). Pulmonary nodules at diagnosis were the only predictor associated with the development of an SPLC (hazard ratio [HR] 2.37; 95% CI 1.09-5.13; p = 0.029), although this association weakened and lost significance when the analysis was restricted to metachronous tumors (HR 1.84; 95% CI 0.71-4.77; p = 0.207). Metachronous tumors were predominantly squamous cell carcinomas (83.3%), whereas adenocarcinoma was the most common histological type among synchronous tumors (50.0%; p = 0.022). Patients with SPLC had a shorter overall survival than those without it (median 5.4 vs. 8.0 years; log-rank p = 0.016). The presence of pulmonary nodules at LSCC diagnosis was associated with a higher risk of SPLC. However, these findings originate from a single center, and further studies are needed to determine whether stratification based on initial radiological findings can improve early detection of SPLC in patients with LSCC.

title: Beyond the Green Veil: Residential Accessibility to Urban Green-Blue Spaces and Cause-Specific Mortality-An Ecological Study of 37 Polish Cities.
authors: Czernych R, Berezowski T, Badyda A et al.
abstract: Background/Objectives: Urban green and blue spaces are increasingly recognized for their potential health benefits, but evidence on their associations with cause-specific mortality in Central and Eastern Europe remains limited. This study examined the association between residential accessibility to green-blue spaces and cause-specific mortality across 37 large Polish cities. We hypothesized that residential proximity would be more strongly associated with health outcomes than overall green-blue space coverage. Methods: This ecological cross-sectional study used mortality and hospitalization data for 2015-2019 and spatial data from the CORINE Land Cover 2018 database. We compared two exposure metrics: availability (the proportion of city area classified as green-blue space) and accessibility (mean residential distance to these spaces). Quasi-Poisson generalized linear models (GLMs) and generalized additive models (GAMs) were used to estimate adjusted mortality and hospitalization rate ratios for cardiovascular diseases, cerebrovascular diseases, malignant neoplasms, and respiratory diseases. The models were adjusted for PM2.5, unemployment, and healthcare availability. Results: Models based on residential distance generally showed better fit than models based on total green-blue area coverage. A 1-SD decrease in residential distance was associated with lower mortality from cardiovascular diseases (MRR = 0.895), cerebrovascular diseases (MRR = 0.842), stroke (MRR = 0.849), and malignant neoplasms (MRR = 0.946). GAMs showed nonlinear patterns, with local troughs around 500-600 m in several strata, but no single consistent threshold. Shorter distance was also associated with lower hospitalization rates for colorectal cancer, lung cancer, prostate cancer, and respiratory diseases. The strongest inverse subgroup estimates were observed among women younger than 65 years; formal interaction tests are needed to determine whether differences between groups are statistically significant. Conclusions: Shorter residential distance to urban green-blue infrastructure was associated with lower mortality for selected causes of death. These findings suggest that equitable access to natural environments may be relevant to urban planning and could complement strategies focused solely on increasing the total area of green space.

title: Tumor-Secreted microRNAs as Circulating Biomarkers for Lung Cancer Detection and Prognostic Stratification.
authors: Dutta P, Zhang L, Li J et al.
abstract: Background: Early lung cancer detection remains challenging. Low-dose CT screening reduces mortality but is limited by false positives and low uptake. Circulating miRNAs are stable blood biomarkers, but reproducibility is poor as most derive from non-tumor tissues. We hypothesized that miRNAs secreted by lung cancer cells would provide more grounded biomarkers. Methods: Small RNA sequencing was performed on paired intracellular and extracellular RNA from conditioned media of six NSCLC cell lines and non-malignant controls. Differentially expressed miRNAs enriched in cancer-derived fractions were identified. Candidates were validated in serum from NSCLC patients and controls by RT-qPCR and examined in TCGA cohorts. Pathway and survival analyses assessed relevance. Results: Extracellular miRNA profiles were conserved across NSCLC lines and distinct from intracellular profiles. A core set of 25 miRNAs was enriched in cancer-derived media. Five miRNAs (miR-10b, miR-25, miR-92a, miR-182, miR-375) were elevated in NSCLC serum and robustly expressed in TCGA tumors. Pathway analysis showed enrichment of PI3K-Akt and hypoxia signaling. Elevated miR-10b was associated with poorer survival. Conclusions: Lung cancer cells secrete a conserved miRNA set detectable in serum and tumors, linked to oncogenic pathways and survival. Cell-based profiling offers a strategy for developing plasma miRNA assays for lung cancer detection.

title: Evidence-Based Interventions to Address Lung Cancer Prevention Among Women in Appalachia: A Scoping Review.
authors: Thompson JR, Hiscox H, Sotelo-Tornero M et al.
abstract:
INTRODUCTION: Despite the high incidence and mortality rates of lung cancer among women in Appalachia, research on lung cancer prevention in this population is limited. We sought to identify and summarize existing evidence-based interventions that address primary and secondary prevention of lung cancer among women in Appalachia.
METHODS: In 2023, we conducted a scoping review of 5 bibliographic databases (PubMed, CINAHL, PsycINFO, Web of Science, and Cochrane Database for Systematic Reviews) and the gray literature for original research articles, clinical trials, or reviews focused on primary and secondary prevention of lung cancer among adult women in Appalachia. Two coders reviewed the articles to extract overarching information about each study, including design, population, methods, and findings.
RESULTS: We identified 21 articles; most studies described interventions focused on tobacco use cessation, and a few addressed smoke-free laws, radon exposure, or lung cancer screening. Most studies included female participants who currently smoke, including during pregnancy; a few focused on nonsmokers or specific stages of the life course. Study findings indicated potential approaches for addressing structural and cost barriers and combine nonphysician support (eg, community health workers), pharmacotherapy, and community-based strategies.
CONCLUSION: A combination of personalized, sustainable, and culturally relevant strategies may be required to prevent lung cancer among women in Appalachia. Novel studies are needed to uncover ways to improve rates of tobacco use cessation and incorporate screening for radon risk and lung cancer.

title: Artificial Intelligence (AI) in Non-Small Cell Lung Cancer and Immunotherapy: A Review of the Emerging Uses and Current Challenges.
authors: Nangoli S, Lee M
abstract: Lung cancer remains the leading cause of cancer-related mortality worldwide despite major therapeutic advances, including immune checkpoint inhibitors (ICIs). Although a subset of patients with advanced non-small cell lung cancer (NSCLC) experiences durable long-term responses, currently available predictive biomarkers, including programmed death ligand-1 (PD-L1) expression, have limited ability to reliably distinguish responders from non-responders. Artificial intelligence (AI) and machine learning (ML) have emerged as powerful approaches for extracting clinically meaningful patterns from complex, high-dimensional datasets spanning pathology, liquid biopsy, imaging, and integrated multimodal data. This narrative review examines current applications of AI in NSCLC immunotherapy across these complementary data modalities and evaluates the evidence supporting their clinical translation. Particular attention is given to the methodological limitations of existing studies and to the emerging shift from single-modality biomarkers toward dynamic and multimodal prediction. Although AI-based approaches show potential to complement established biomarkers, limitations in validation, generalizability, and prospective evidence currently restrict their clinical implementation.

title: Tissue and Plasma NGS Are Complementary for Molecular Profiling in Advanced Non-Small Cell Lung Cancer: Real-World Concordance and Clinical Impact.
authors: Gómez-Rueda A, Garrido-Lopez P, Pekarek L et al.
abstract: Background: Comprehensive molecular profiling is increasingly important in advanced non-small cell lung cancer (NSCLC), but the integration of tissue- and plasma-based next-generation sequencing (NGS) and its real-world therapeutic impact remain uncertain. Methods: We conducted a retrospective single-center study of 205 patients with advanced NSCLC treated between January 2016 and January 2019 who underwent routine molecular testing and tissue- and/or plasma-based NGS. Concordance was assessed for clinically relevant genomic alterations, and the impact of NGS on treatment decisions was evaluated. Results: A total of 280 NGS assays were performed. NGS identified potentially actionable genomic alterations in 88 patients (42.9%); in 50 patients (24.4%), potentially actionable genomic alterations were identified by NGS relative to conventional molecular testing. Among 64 patients who underwent both tissue- and plasma-based NGS, overall agreement was 78.1%, with moderate concordance (κ = 0.533). NGS results led to a direct treatment modification in 23 patients (11.2%), including clinical trial enrollment, standard targeted therapy, or compassionate-use treatment. Conclusions: Tissue- and plasma-based NGS provided complementary rather than interchangeable genomic information. The difference between theoretical actionability and actual therapeutic impact highlights the importance of clinical context, timing of testing, and treatment availability when interpreting comprehensive genomic profiling in advanced NSCLC.

title: Epigenetic Plasticity in Lung Cancer Therapy Resistance: Mechanisms, Biomarkers, and Rational Combination Strategies.
authors: Polat BE, Ramchandran RM, Yang J et al.
abstract: Lung cancer resistance is commonly attributed to acquired genetic alterations, including on-target mutations, activation of bypass pathways, tumor-suppressor loss, and histologic or lineage transformation. However, genetic evolution alone cannot fully account for the rapid, reversible, and heterogeneous adaptations that emerge during treatment. Epigenetic plasticity, mediated through DNA methylation, histone modifications, chromatin-remodeling complexes, and transcriptional state transitions, enables tumor cells to enter drug-tolerant states, alter lineage identity, evade immune surveillance, and persist under therapeutic pressure, creating conditions in which more stable forms of resistance can develop. This review examines how epigenetic programs interact with oncogenic drivers and tumor-suppressor loss to shape therapy resistance across lung cancer. We discuss chromatin-mediated resistance to targeted therapies, cytotoxic chemotherapy, and immune checkpoint blockade, with particular attention to drug-tolerant persister states, epithelial-mesenchymal and neuroendocrine transitions, impaired antigen presentation, and remodeling of the tumor microenvironment. We critically assess the evidence for DNA methyltransferase and histone deacetylase inhibitors, together with emerging strategies targeting EZH2/EZH1, LSD1, BET proteins, PRMT5/MAT2A, and vulnerabilities associated with SWI/SNF dysfunction. Clinical translation has been limited by modest single-agent activity, treatment-related toxicity, incomplete pharmacodynamic assessment, and inadequate biomarker-based patient selection. Future progress will depend on matching epigenetic interventions to defined biological states, confirming intratumoral target engagement, and integrating longitudinal multiomic profiling to guide patient selection, treatment sequencing, and early interception of emerging resistance.
