title: The Role of One-Month Surveillance MRI After Stereotactic Radiosurgery for Brain Metastases.
authors: Hughes KO, McClelland S
abstract:
OBJECTIVES: Surveillance MRI after stereotactic radiosurgery (SRS) for brain metastases is often deferred until 3 months post-SRS. We evaluated the incidence, characteristics, and management of new brain metastases on routine MRI obtained 1 month after SRS.
METHODS: We retrospectively reviewed 99 SRS courses in 68 patients treated between March 2025 and September 2026. A 1-month MRI was defined as routine surveillance imaging 30±14 days after the first SRS treatment. All new lesions were confirmed by radiation oncology and neuroradiology review. Associations were assessed using the Fisher exact test, with patient-level and clustered sensitivity analyses.
RESULTS: Forty-seven courses in 33 patients had a 1-month MRI. New metastases were identified in 23 courses (49%; 95% CI: 35%-63%), with 74 new lesions; 16 of 23 (70%) had 1 to 3 lesions. The median largest new lesion was 4 mm (range: 2 to 26), and 4 of 20 (20%) measured 15 mm or larger. Additional brain radiotherapy followed in 22 of 23 courses, including repeat SRS in 19. New metastases were more frequent with lung than nonlung primaries (65% vs. 29%; clustered odds ratio 4.7, 95% CI: 1.5-15.1), including at the patient level (69% vs. 24%; P=0.015). No significant difference was detected by number of metastases treated, prior SRS, platform, or age.
CONCLUSIONS: New brain metastases were common on routine MRI 1 month after SRS, particularly in patients with lung cancer. Whether earlier detection improves neurological outcomes or survival is unknown, and prospective evaluation of early surveillance in lung cancer is warranted.

title: AMMR-Surv: Learning Metabolic and Morphologic Responses Across Lesions from Longitudinal PET/CT for Survival Prediction in Non-Small-Cell Lung Cancer.
authors: Lv J, Zhang Q, Liao Z et al.
abstract: Lesion responses to chemoradiotherapy can differ within a patient, complicating prognostic assessment in locally advanced non-small-cell lung cancer. We developed AMMR-Surv to integrate prototype-based metabolic response learning, asymmetric CT comparison, and event-aware multi-lesion aggregation. This retrospective study included 126 patients from ACRIN 6668/RTOG 0235 with paired fluorodeoxyglucose positron emission tomography/computed tomography (FDG-PET/CT) before and after treatment. Overall survival was measured from post-treatment examination. Five-fold nested patient-level cross-validation was repeated five times, with prototype counts selected within each outer training partition. Aggregated out-of-fold Uno's concordance was 0.719 (95% confidence interval [CI], 0.670-0.772), with a 24-month area under the curve of 0.765 and an integrated Brier score of 0.1747. Paired concordance differences were 0.007 (95% CI, -0.021 to 0.046) versus generic longitudinal modeling and 0.059 (95% CI, 0.005-0.114) versus clinical variables with simple PET measurements. Across three runs on 120 common lesion sites, aligned prototype-assignment agreement ranged from 93.33% to 96.67%. These results support further evaluation of lesion-response representations, although superiority over generic longitudinal modeling remains uncertain. The small, selected cohort limits generalizability, and earlier fixed-four-prototype analyses remain exploratory because that configuration was selected using test performance. Independent validation is required before clinical application.

title: Therapeutic antibodies targeting PD-1 or PD-L1 impact the circulation time of soluble checkpoint receptor/ligand targets.
authors: Micke P, Lord M, Isaksson J et al.
abstract: Using OLINK PEA and Meso Scale Discovery, MSD, we quantified soluble PD-1 (sPD-1) and PD-L1 (sPD-L1) in lung cancer patients receiving pembrolizumab, nivolumab or atezolizumab monotherapy. Elevated sPD-1 and sPD-L1 levels were significantly therapy-dependent; pembrolizumab and nivolumab increased sPD-1, while atezolizumab increased sPD-L1. Thus, elevated levels may reflect therapeutic antibody-mediated half-life extension via antibody-soluble target complex formation, rather than solely biologically induced target shedding or production.

title: Pulmonary Sarcoidosis Mimicking Multifocal Adenocarcinoma: An Atypical Radiologic and Diagnostic Dilemma.
authors: Gohar A, Hmeedan A, Saeed A et al.
abstract: Known as "the great mimic," sarcoidosis often poses a diagnostic challenge. Although common radiological manifestations include hilar and mediastinal lymphadenopathy and micronodules, atypical patterns can also be encountered, requiring awareness of the disease's potential radiological manifestations to allow for prompt diagnosis and management. We report a case of sarcoidosis presenting with predominant ground-glass opacities (GGOs) on high-resolution CT (HRCT) of the chest, mimicking adenocarcinoma in situ. The diagnosis was established by histopathology after other causes of pulmonary GGOs had been excluded. This report highlights the importance of maintaining a high degree of clinical suspicion and pursuing a comprehensive workup, including tissue diagnosis, even in minimally symptomatic patients.

title: Folate-functionalized mesoporous silica nanoparticles for co-delivery of doxorubicin and myricetin to overcome doxorubicin resistance in non-small cell lung cancer cells.
authors: Govindaraj R, Kotteeswaran V
abstract: The non-small cell lung cancer (NSCLC) remains the leading cause of cancer-related mortality, with multidrug resistance (MDR) severely limiting the efficacy of chemotherapy. Doxorubicin (DOX) resistance is primarily mediated by enhanced drug efflux and activation of antioxidant and pro-survival signalling pathways. Here, a DOX-resistant A549/DOX cell model was established by stepwise DOX dose escalation to evaluate whether folic acid-functionalized mesoporous silica nanoparticles co-loaded with DOX and myricetin (FA-MSN-DOX-MYR) can overcome acquired chemoresistance. FA-MSN-DOX-MYR showed enhanced, time-dependent intracellular accumulation, greater cytotoxicity (IC50 = 0.8 μg/mL), inhibition of clonogenic survival, and spheroid growth compared with free DOX and non-folate formulations. Mechanistically, FA-MSN-DOX-MYR increased intracellular ROS, induced mitochondrial dysfunction and caspase-3-dependent apoptosis, and downregulated MDR1/P-glycoprotein (7-fold), Nrf2 (4.5-fold), NF-κB (2-fold), and p-Akt, which was associated with restored chemosensitivity. In addition, FA-MSN-DOX-MYR had less cytotoxicity than free DOX in H9c2 cardiomyocytes, suggesting reduced cardiotoxicity. Collectively, these findings suggest that folate-functionalized co-delivery of DOX and myricetin effectively reverses MDR by suppressing drug efflux and pro-survival signalling while enhancing oxidative stress-mediated apoptosis. This research evidence warrants that FA-MSN-DOX-MYR will be a promising nanomedicine for multidrug-resistant NSCLC.

title: Antitumor Effects of a Small Artificial RNA Sequence in Malignant Pleural Mesothelioma Through Suppression of Cell Cycle-Related Transcriptional Programs.
authors: Kouda S, Yamamoto H, Uchida R et al.
abstract: Background/Objectives: Malignant pleural mesothelioma (MPM) is an aggressive malignancy with a poor prognosis and limited therapeutic options. Small RNA-based therapeutics may provide a means of simultaneously modulating multiple oncogenic pathways. We screened candidate small RNAs for antitumor activity in MPM and investigated the molecular basis of the response to the selected sequence. We aimed to identify a small RNA with reproducible antitumor activity in human mesothelioma cells and to define the signaling and transcriptional programs associated with its activity. Methods: Candidate small RNAs were transfected into three human mesothelioma cell lines (H2052, H2452, and H28). Cell viability and proliferation were assessed by WST-8 and BrdU incorporation assays. Intracellular signaling was examined using dual-luciferase reporters, and RNA sequencing with gene set enrichment analysis (GSEA) was used to characterize transcriptional changes. Results: Among the tested RNAs, the small artificial sequence (SAS) most consistently reduced cell viability and significantly suppressed proliferation in all three cell lines. Untreated mesothelioma cells showed prominent enrichment of E2F Targets compared with normal lung tissue, whereas SAS treatment suppressed E2F-associated cell-cycle programs and significantly reduced BrdU incorporation, consistent with inhibition of G1/S cell-cycle progression. SAS also reduced AP1 and SRE activities in H2452 cells but not in H2052 cells, indicating cell line-dependent modulation of MAPK-related signaling. SAS also induced interferon- and inflammatory response gene sets, with particularly strong cytokine induction observed after phosphorothioate (PS) modification of the passenger strand. Conclusions: SAS exerted reproducible antitumor effects in human mesothelioma cells, with suppression of cell proliferation and E2F-associated cell-cycle programs as the most consistent findings. These results support further investigation of SAS in MPM, although its therapeutic efficacy remains to be established in vivo.

title: Disulfidptosis-Related Genes Comprise Two Functionally Distinct, Transcriptionally Uncoupled Subsets with Complementary Prognostic Associations: An Integrated Pan-Cancer Analysis of TCGA Data.
authors: Kus Z, Eslamkhah S, Gulmez H et al.
abstract: Disulfidptosis is a regulated form of cell death that arises from NADPH depletion and disulfide stress on the actin cytoskeleton in cells with high SLC7A11. Scores built from disulfidptosis-related genes (DRGs) are increasingly put forward as prognostic markers, yet their internal structure and metabolic context have remained poorly defined. We examined 24 DRGs across 10,242 primary tumours (33 TCGA cancer types) and 722 normal tissues, drawing on survival, purity and genomic data. SLC7A11 was up-regulated in 14 of 18 cancers, while the majority of cytoskeletal DRGs sat at lower levels in tumours. The DRG score showed a heterogeneous pooled link to shorter overall survival (HR per SD 1.15, 95% CI 1.06-1.25; prediction interval 0.78-1.70) and stayed associated after adjustment for available clinical covariates and purity in six cancers (FDR < 0.05): adverse in five, among them lower-grade glioma (HR 1.68; attenuated to 1.24, p = 0.046, after adjustment for IDH and 1p/19q status, grade and purity) and mesothelioma, and protective in clear-cell renal carcinoma. The predefined core and cytoskeleton subsets were almost uncorrelated (median ρ = -0.04): SLC7A11 expression tracked pentose phosphate/NADPH genes independently of purity (median ρ = 0.32), whereas the cytoskeleton subset ran opposite to oxidative phosphorylation genes. After adjustment for NRF2 target expression, however, SLC7A11 was not more strongly coupled to core PPP enzyme genes than expression-matched random genes. In joint models, each subset proved independently prognostic, but in different cancers. The composite score was prognostic in more cancer types than random gene sets of equal size (9 vs. 3; p = 0.04), whereas in the four cancers with robust models, DRG-based LASSO-Cox models performed no better than models built from random 24-gene sets. DRG scores are better decomposed than read as a single disulfidptosis axis.

title: Exosome-Based Therapeutic Perspectives in Pleural Mesothelioma: A Double-Edged Sword with Biological Opportunities and Translational Challenges.
authors: Cortes-Dericks L, Galetta D
abstract: Pleural mesothelioma (PM) is an aggressive malignancy with limited therapeutic options, underscoring the need for novel therapeutic alternatives. Exosomes, a subset of extracellular vesicles mediating intercellular communication, have emerged as potential therapeutic platforms due to their ability to transfer functional biomolecules and modulate cellular responses. In PM, however, exosomes exert context-dependent effects: tumor-derived exosomes actively contribute to tumor progression, immune modulation, and therapy resistance, while exosomes of non-tumor origin or those subjected to engineering approaches may be exploited for targeted therapeutic delivery. This review discusses the mechanistic foundations of exosome biology relevant to PM and current preclinical efforts to harness exosomes as carriers of nucleic acids, small molecules, and immune-modulatory agents. It further evaluates the influence of exosome cell-of-origin and the intrinsic therapeutic paradox arising from the dual biological roles of exosomes. Finally, key translational challenges, including optimization of exosome source, cargo loading efficiency and manufacturing scalability, are examined as major obstacles to clinical implementation. Addressing these challenges is essential for translating exosome-based strategies into more effective therapeutic interventions in this malignancy.

title: MX1 Expression in Cancer Cells Is Strongly Linked to CD8+ T-Cell Infiltration and PD-L1 Expression: A Tissue Microarray Study Evaluating More than 14,000 Tumors from 145 Different Tumor Entities.
authors: Bajusz B, Hinsch A, Büyücek S et al.
abstract: Introduction: Myxovirus resistance protein 1 (MX1) contributes to resistance against viral infections, including to influenza, and has recently been implicated in cancer. Methods: A tissue microarray with 17,909 samples from 145 tumor types/subtypes and 608 samples from 76 normal tissue types was analyzed by immunohistochemistry (IHC) to assess MX1 expression. Results: MX1 positivity was found in tumor cells of 5956 of 14,512 analyzable samples, and 131 of 145 entities included at least one positive case. High positivity rates occurred in squamous cell carcinomas (up to 88%), neuroendocrine neoplasms (up to 85%), germ cell neoplasms (up to 77%), salivary gland tumors (up to 75%), mesothelioma (up to 74%), endometrial and ovarian carcinomas (up to 73%), cervical adenocarcinoma (73%), pancreatic ductal adenocarcinoma (65%), and urothelial carcinoma (up to 62%). MX1 expression correlated with PD-L1 positivity and CD8+ lymphocyte density (p < 0.0001 each). High MX1 expression was linked to grade progression in breast cancer (p < 0.0001), microsatellite instability in colorectal adenocarcinoma (p = 0.0003), high grade (p = 0.0431) and advanced pT stage (p = 0.0269) in hepatocellular carcinoma, distant metastasis in clear cell renal cell carcinoma (ccRCC, p = 0.0164), and nodal metastasis in papillary RCC (pRCC; p = 0.0326). Low MX1 expression was linked to stage progression in muscle-invasive urothelial carcinoma (p = 0.0372) and colorectal adenocarcinoma (p = 0.0002), papillary (p = 0.013) and follicular (p = 0.0221) thyroid cancer, and nodal metastasis in serous high-grade ovarian carcinoma (p = 0.0355). MX1 expression was unrelated to phenotype in endometrioid endometrial and ovarian carcinoma. Conclusions: MX1 expression in tumors is strongly linked to CD8+ lymphocyte density and PD-L1 expression, suggesting an association with an immune-inflamed, type I interferon-related tumor microenvironment.

title: Combined dopamine receptor inhibition and radiotherapy target mesothelioma-initiating cells and increase survival in a mouse model of mesothelioma.
authors: Cardenas A, Arambula E, Azizi L et al.
abstract:
INTRODUCTION: Malignant pleural mesothelioma (MPM) is a rare thoracic cancer associated with poor prognosis and low survival rates. In solid cancers, repurposed dopamine receptor antagonists have been shown to have anti-cancer effects. Moreover, in combination with radiotherapy, quetiapine (QTP), a dopamine 2/3 receptor antagonist, has been shown to interfere with self-renewal capacity in glioma-initiating cells and increase survival in mouse models of glioblastoma. In this study we explore combined treatment effects in MPM.
METHODS: Using mesothelioma cell lines, MSTO-211H, H2052, and H2452, and a MSTO-211H-derived orthotopic xenograft mouse model of MPM we examined how QTP combined with radiation affects mesothelioma-initiating cells (MICs) in vitro and survival in vivo. Subsequently, bulk and single cell RNA sequencing was used to characterize the transcriptomic landscape of MSTO-211H treated with combined radiation and QTP.
RESULTS: We demonstrate that combining QTP with radiation reduces MIC self-renewal capacity and stem cell frequency. In vivo, this combination therapy significantly extends the median survival of mesothelioma-bearing mice. Clonogenic survival assays revealed that QTP does not enhance radiosensitivity. Sequencing data revealed, combined treatment downregulated cell cycle and proliferation pathways, depleted cancer stem cells, and increased cellular senescence.
CONCLUSION: Taken together, our study highlights the therapeutic potential of radiation with QTP in the treatment of MPM.

title: Cholesterol and high concentration serum cooperatively enhance canine CAR T cell transduction and expansion
summary: Chimeric antigen receptor (CAR) T cell immunotherapy is emerging as a promising adjunct treatment option for refractory canine cancers. Unfortunately, clinical trials thus far have failed to meaningfully reduce tumor burden, highlighting the need for improved CAR T cell manufacturing strategies. Effective autologous therapy requires highly viable, efficiently transduced T cells capable of robust expansion, sustained CAR expression, and long-term persistence. Although these parameters have been extensively investigated in humans, comparable optimization in canine systems remains limited. Here, we evaluated culture conditions to improve canine T cell expansion, memory differentiation, and retroviral transduction efficiency. We demonstrated IL-2 supplementation supported superior cellular expansion and preservation of less-differentiated memory phenotypes compared to IL-7 with IL-15. Additionally, we found that increasing cell density during shorter stimulation periods improved expansion while also driving better T cell transduction rates. We discovered that the addition of cholesterol and high-concentration fetal bovine serum (FBS) to media during the transduction period reliably and markedly enhanced transduction efficiency following a single round of retroviral transduction, even at elevated temperatures that would otherwise impair transduction efficiency. This enhancement was observed with both GALV- and RD114-pseudotyped retroviruses and was accompanied by a marked improvement in cellular expansion without driving terminal differentiation of T cell subsets that are prone to exhaustion in vivo. Collectively, these findings identify practical strategies to improve canine CAR T-cell manufacturing and advance the development of clinically viable CAR T cells for canine cancer treatment.
